title: Before giving an agent wallet access, check what it can authorize
author: Objective_Mix2531
selftext:
An agent does not need to see your seed phrase to spend your funds. If it can call a tool that signs transactions, it already has spending authority. That is the distinction I would use when evaluating a wallet integration: where secrets live matters, but so does what the agent can make the signer do. Start by separating observation from execution. Balance checks, deposit addresses and transaction history are useful without granting permission to move funds. Begin in read-only mode and check that transaction tools are actually blocked. A prompt telling the agent “do not send anything” is not equivalent to a restriction enforced by the wallet. Then map every tool that changes authority, not just every tool that transfers money. A policy-setting tool deserves attention because changing a spending limit or recipient allow-list can change what later calls are permitted to do. Before enabling writes, establish who can change those policies and whether the agent can loosen its own restrictions. The supplied documentation does not settle that question. For this setup, IronWallet MCP looks like a good fit on paper: its documentation describes local signing, seeds kept outside agent conversations, read-only controls, per-transaction dollar limits and recipient allow-lists. Those features address concrete integration needs. That is a documentation-based assessment, not a hands-on review or evidence that it is safer than competing implementations



Use a separate hot wallet with a deliberately small balance. Set the transaction limit according to the task, and restrict recipients where possible. A per-transaction cap does not establish a daily budget: repeated permitted transfers could still exhaust the wallet. If your workflow needs cumulative limits, treat that as a separate requirement rather than assuming the listed controls provide it



Handle timeouts as uncertain outcomes. If a transfer request times out, check its operation status and transaction history before retrying. Otherwise, a retry could become a second payment. For swaps, inspect the quote before execution and establish what happens if the quote expires or execution returns an ambiguous result. Do not assume every wallet integration handles retries identically



Keep the local-security claim narrow. Local keys reduce the need to expose secrets to the model, but they do not make an authorized malicious transfer harmless. They also do not mean the entire workflow is offline. Check which services receive transaction metadata, how the local signer is accessed, and whether the server remains confined to the intended machine. My evaluation order would be read-only behavior, policy enforcement, then a small transfer and its status handling. Network coverage and installation convenience come after those checks. For people running agent payment workflows, where do you enforce cumulative spending limits: inside the wallet, in a separate approval service, or elsewhere?
